sm: Host Kato Dal of the Wall Street Journal's Potomac Watch talks with Matthew Kroenig, president of a firm he started with former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, about President Trump's planned meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping on the sidelines of a conference in China. Trump has said nuclear weapons will be a main topic. Kroenig says Trump is right to seek talks, since there are currently no arms control agreements limiting the superpowers, but he expects little success. China has never seriously negotiated and is building toward a thousand warheads by 2030 and fifteen hundred by 2035. He says the buildup may serve a Taiwan strategy and prestige. He and the host agree Trump was right to let New START expire.

Kroenig says New START, signed in 2010, no longer fits today's environment. He can imagine trilateral deals in the American interest, such as limiting Russian and Chinese battlefield nuclear weapons, banning exotic systems like Russia's nuclear-armed submarine drone and China's fractional orbital bombardment test, or capping China at about two hundred warheads. He doubts Putin or Xi would agree, so the value is showing the world they are the problem. On battlefield weapons, he says Russia has around two thousand and an escalate-to-deescalate strategy, while China's are mostly theater missiles. China officially has a no-first-use policy, but Pentagon officials doubt it, and he worries about Taiwan.

Asked what conditions allow arms control, Kroenig notes Trump has been interested since the 1980s. Historically, big breakthroughs came late in the Cold War as tensions fell, and he thinks we are at the start of a second Cold War, with years or decades of buildup ahead. He served on the bipartisan Strategic Posture Commission, whose 2023 report called for an arms buildup because the US must deter two nuclear peers. The 1,550 deployed warhead limit is not enough, and the commission urged more non-strategic weapons in Europe and Asia. He cites the sea-launched nuclear cruise missile, which Congress funded despite Biden administration objections, and is cautiously optimistic about bipartisan support. The host then raises the Golden Dome missile shield.

Kroenig dismisses the idea that leaving the US homeland vulnerable is wise, since Russia and China build their own defenses and a shield could blunt limited coercive strikes. He says cheap space launch makes space-based sensors and interceptors affordable now, and the commission backed missile defense. On allies, he says the US nuclear umbrella covers more than thirty treaty allies and aims to dissuade proliferation, and a majority of South Koreans favor their own weapons, so Washington should keep reassuring Seoul. He supports the Iran war and hopes Trump privately presses Russia and China to stop aiding Iran. He says this is unlike Yalta because the meeting is with enemies. He calls US nuclear weapons secure because they are air gapped and old.
